title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–4)
hook: Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha in the kitchen and Mary at his feet. Your line was one thing is needful. Did you manage to sit before you served? Day five hundred forty-three.

Luke keeps noticing something the other Gospels mention less often: Jesus praying. At his baptism, before choosing the twelve, on the mountain when his face changed. Today it happens again. He is praying in a certain place, and his friends wait nearby until he finishes. Picture them, standing a little way off, watching someone talk to God as if God were right there. When he stops, one of them asks a question. Not about miracles, not about the kingdom, not about who's the greatest. Just this: show us how.

In the King James Bible, the disciple says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." Teachers in that world often gave their followers a prayer of their own, a kind of family signature. John the Baptist had done it. Now they want theirs. And what Jesus gives in Luke is short. The King James text of Luke reads much like Matthew's, but many of the oldest Greek manuscripts of Luke have a shorter prayer, and most modern translations follow them. It opens with one word: Father. Then five requests. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Bread for each day. Forgiveness. And protection from the time of trial. That's it. You could say it in fifteen seconds. Two small differences from Matthew are worth hearing. Luke's bread line in the King James is "Give us day by day our daily bread." Day by day: not a stockpile, a habit. And where Matthew says debts, Luke says: "And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us." Sins for us, debts for others, as if our own wrongs were the bigger account. One more surprise: the famous ending, for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory, isn't in Luke at all. Churches added it as a closing of praise. Many Protestant churches say it straight after the prayer; in the Catholic Mass it comes a moment later, after another short prayer by the priest. So the prayer many Christians know by heart grew from a short answer to a simple request. Teach us.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray Luke's version, slowly. Settle and breathe. If you pray, you can say the King James lines one per breath, leaving long gaps: Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Give us day by day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation. If you don't pray, take just one of those five requests and sit with it. Which one names something you actually need today? Bread, forgiveness, protection? Let it stay with you until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Teach us to pray. A disciple's request after watching Jesus pray, and Luke's short answer: one word, Father, and five requests.
Your line: teach us. Today, ask someone to show you one thing they do well, and listen like a student. Day five hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Christians around the world pray the Lord's Prayer daily, usually in Matthew's longer form; many Protestant churches add the closing doxology straight after it, while the Catholic Mass places the doxology after a short prayer by the priest.

original.note: Greek: Father. in many of the oldest manuscripts, Luke's prayer begins with this one word.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Lord's Prayer is the same everywhere in the Bible.
what it means: Luke gives a shorter prayer, Father and five requests, as Jesus' answer to a disciple's request.
what a scholar hears: the King James text of Luke follows later manuscripts that match Matthew; older ones are shorter, and the doxology is in neither Luke nor the oldest copies of Matthew.
